notes:
Zeroth & first law

  • Zeroth law: if A and B are separately in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other — basis of temperature measurement.
  • First law: $\Delta Q = \Delta U + \Delta W$ (heat given $=$ change in internal energy $+$ work done by the gas). Internal energy $U$ depends only on temperature for an ideal gas (state function).

Thermodynamic processes

ProcessConditionWork done by gas
Isothermal$T$ constant, $PV=$ const$W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$; $\Delta U = 0$
Adiabatic$Q=0$, $PV^\gamma=$ const$W = \dfrac{nR(T_1-T_2)}{\gamma-1}$
Isobaric$P$ constant$W = P\Delta V = nR\Delta T$
Isochoric$V$ constant$W = 0$
  • Slope of adiabatic curve is steeper than isothermal at a given point ($\gamma>1$).
  • Work done by gas $=$ area under $P$-$V$ curve; in a cyclic process $\Delta U=0$ so $Q_{net}=W_{net}=$ area enclosed by the loop.

Specific heats of gas

  • $C_P - C_V = R$ (Mayer's relation, per mole); $\gamma = C_P/C_V$. Monatomic: $C_V=\tfrac32R$, $C_P=\tfrac52R$, $\gamma=5/3$. Diatomic: $C_V=\tfrac52R$, $C_P=\tfrac72R$, $\gamma=7/5$.

Second law & heat engines

  • Kelvin-Planck statement: no engine can convert heat completely into work with no other effect (100% efficiency impossible).
  • Clausius statement: heat cannot flow spontaneously from a colder to a hotter body without external work.
  • Heat engine efficiency: $\eta = \dfrac{W}{Q_1} = 1-\dfrac{Q_2}{Q_1}$ ($Q_1$ = heat absorbed from source, $Q_2$ = heat rejected to sink).
  • Carnot engine (ideal, reversible): $\eta_{Carnot} = 1-\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$ (temperatures in kelvin) — the maximum possible efficiency between $T_1$ and $T_2$.
  • Refrigerator/heat pump: coefficient of performance $\text{COP} = \dfrac{Q_2}{W} = \dfrac{T_2}{T_1-T_2}$.

Exam tip

KCET typically asks 2 questions — one numerical on efficiency/Carnot engine or work done in isothermal/adiabatic process, and one conceptual question on the first/second law or sign conventions. Remember: $Q$ and $W$ positive when heat is added to / work is done by the gas.

questions.q: In a thermodynamic process, 500 J of heat is supplied to a gas and the gas does 200 J of work on the surroundings. The change in internal energy of the gas is
questions.explanation: First law: $\Delta U = \Delta Q - \Delta W = 500-200 = 300$ J.
questions.trick: First law: $\Delta U=\Delta Q-\Delta W$ — heat in minus work done by gas.

questions.q: For an ideal gas undergoing an isothermal process, the change in internal energy is
questions.explanation: Internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on temperature; since $T$ is constant in an isothermal process, $\Delta U=0$.
questions.trick: Ideal gas $U$ depends only on $T$; isothermal $\Rightarrow\Delta T=0\Rightarrow\Delta U=0$.

questions.q: In an adiabatic process, if the gas expands, then
questions.explanation: Adiabatic means $Q=0$. On expansion the gas does positive work using its internal energy ($\Delta U = -W$), so its temperature falls.
questions.trick: Adiabatic expansion: gas does work using its own $U$, so temperature drops.

questions.q: One mole of an ideal gas expands isothermally at temperature $T$ from volume $V$ to $2V$. The work done by the gas is
questions.explanation: $W = nRT\ln(V_2/V_1) = RT\ln(2V/V) = RT\ln 2$.
questions.trick: Isothermal work $W=nRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$ — here $V_2/V_1=2$, so $RT\ln2$.

questions.q: For a monatomic ideal gas, the ratio of specific heats $\gamma = C_P/C_V$ is
questions.explanation: Monatomic gas: $C_V = \tfrac32R$, $C_P=\tfrac52R$, so $\gamma = 5/3$.
questions.trick: Memorise: monatomic $\gamma=5/3$, diatomic $\gamma=7/5$.

questions.q: For one mole of an ideal gas, $C_P - C_V$ equals
questions.explanation: Mayer's relation: $C_P - C_V = R$ for one mole of an ideal gas.
questions.trick: Mayer's relation: $C_P-C_V=R$ per mole — a fixed constant, memorise it.

questions.q: On a $P$-$V$ diagram, at a given point, compared to the isothermal curve through that point, the adiabatic curve is
questions.explanation: Slope of isothermal $=-P/V$; slope of adiabatic $=-\gamma P/V$. Since $\gamma>1$, the adiabatic curve is steeper at the point of intersection.
questions.trick: Adiabatic slope $=-\gamma P/V$, steeper than isothermal's $-P/V$ since $\gamma>1$.

questions.q: A Carnot engine operates between a source at 600 K and a sink at 300 K. Its efficiency is
questions.trick: Carnot: $\eta=1-T_2/T_1$ — plug kelvin temperatures directly.

questions.q: A Carnot engine absorbs 800 J of heat from a source at 500 K and rejects heat to a sink at 300 K. The work done by the engine per cycle is
questions.trick: Find $\eta=1-T_2/T_1$ first, then $W=\eta Q_1$.

questions.q: According to the Kelvin-Planck statement of the second law of thermodynamics
options: heat cannot flow from a cold body to a hot body on its own
entropy of an isolated system always decreases
no engine can have 100% efficiency by converting all absorbed heat into work with no other effect
the internal energy of an isolated system is constant
questions.explanation: Kelvin-Planck statement: it is impossible to construct an engine operating in a cycle that converts heat completely into work, with no other effect. Option A ('heat cannot flow from a cold body to a hot body on its own') is the Clausius statement.
questions.trick: Kelvin-Planck = no 100% efficient engine; Clausius = no heat flow cold$\to$hot alone.

questions.q: A refrigerator works between 260 K (freezer) and 300 K (room). Its coefficient of performance is
questions.trick: $\text{COP}=T_2/(T_1-T_2)$ — plug the cold and hot reservoir temperatures.

questions.q: In a cyclic process, the net change in internal energy of the system is
options: equal to the net heat absorbed only if adiabatic
questions.explanation: Internal energy is a state function; after a complete cycle the system returns to its initial state, so $\Delta U_{net}=0$, and hence $Q_{net}=W_{net}$.
questions.trick: Cyclic process returns to start $\Rightarrow\Delta U=0$ always (state function).

questions.q: For an isochoric (constant volume) process, the work done by the gas is
questions.explanation: Since volume does not change, $W=\int P\,dV = 0$.
questions.trick: Constant volume $\Rightarrow$ no $dV\Rightarrow W=\int P\,dV=0$.

questions.q: Two moles of an ideal diatomic gas are heated at constant pressure so that its temperature rises by 20 K. The work done by the gas is (R = 8.3 J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$)
questions.explanation: At constant pressure, $W = nR\Delta T = 2\times8.3\times20 = 332$ J.
questions.trick: Isobaric work $W=nR\Delta T$ — no need for pressure or volume values.

questions.q: The area enclosed by a cyclic process on a $P$-$V$ diagram represents
options: the total internal energy of the gas
the net heat absorbed (or net work done) in the cycle
questions.explanation: For a cyclic process $\Delta U=0$, so the net work done by the gas (equal to net heat absorbed) equals the area enclosed by the closed loop on the $P$-$V$ diagram.
questions.trick: Cyclic loop's enclosed area $=$ net work $=$ net heat absorbed per cycle.

questions.q: A quasi-static process is one that proceeds
options: infinitely fast so that no heat is exchanged
so slowly that the system remains in thermal and mechanical equilibrium throughout
questions.explanation: A quasi-static process occurs slowly enough that the system stays arbitrarily close to equilibrium at each stage, allowing well-defined P, V, T throughout.
questions.trick: Quasi-static = infinitely slow, staying in equilibrium at every intermediate step.

questions.q: If a gas is compressed adiabatically, its temperature
questions.explanation: In adiabatic compression $Q=0$, so all the work done on the gas increases its internal energy, raising the temperature.
questions.trick: Adiabatic compression: work done on gas raises $U\Rightarrow$ temperature rises.

questions.q: No real engine can be more efficient than a Carnot engine operating between the same two temperatures because the Carnot engine is
options: reversible and involves no dissipative losses
questions.explanation: The Carnot engine is an idealized, fully reversible cycle with no friction or dissipation, giving it the maximum possible efficiency $1-T_2/T_1$ between two given temperatures; any real (irreversible) engine is less efficient.
questions.trick: Carnot is reversible with zero dissipation $\Rightarrow$ sets the max efficiency bound.

questions.q: The zeroth law of thermodynamics states that
options: heat flows from cold to hot without external work
energy is conserved in all processes
entropy of the universe always increases
if A and B are separately in thermal equilibrium with C, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other
questions.explanation: This is the statement of the zeroth law; it justifies using a thermometer (C) to compare the temperatures of two bodies (A and B) without bringing them into direct contact.
questions.trick: Zeroth law: A,B each in equilibrium with C $\Rightarrow$ A,B in equilibrium too.

questions.q: One mole of an ideal monatomic gas ($C_V=\tfrac32R$, $R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$) is heated at constant volume so that its temperature rises by 40 K. The heat absorbed by the gas is
questions.explanation: At constant volume $W=0$, so $Q=\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T=1\times(1.5\times8.3)\times40=12.45\times40=498$ J.
questions.trick: Constant volume: $Q=\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T$ (no work term to subtract).

questions.q: Two moles of a diatomic ideal gas ($\gamma=7/5$, $R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$) expand adiabatically, and its temperature falls from 400 K to 300 K. The work done by the gas is
questions.explanation: $W=\dfrac{nR(T_1-T_2)}{\gamma-1}=\dfrac{2\times8.3\times100}{0.4}=4150$ J.
questions.trick: Adiabatic work $W=nR(T_1-T_2)/(\gamma-1)$ — direct formula, plug and go.

questions.q: In the free expansion of an ideal gas into a vacuum (no external pressure to do work against, container thermally insulated), which of the following is true?
options: Temperature of the gas rises, though $Q=0$ and $W=0$
$Q=0$, $W=0$ and hence $\Delta U=0$, so the temperature remains unchanged
questions.explanation: Free expansion is irreversible; no work is done against a vacuum ($W=0$) and the system is insulated ($Q=0$), so by the first law $\Delta U=0$ — for an ideal gas this means the temperature stays the same.
questions.trick: Free expansion: $Q=0,W=0\Rightarrow\Delta U=0\Rightarrow$ temperature unchanged for ideal gas.

questions.q: A reversible thermodynamic process is one that
options: can only occur in a vacuum
always releases heat to the surroundings
can be exactly retraced in the reverse direction, restoring both the system and surroundings to their original states, and consists of a succession of equilibrium states
questions.explanation: A reversible process proceeds through a continuous series of equilibrium states with no dissipative effects (friction, unrestrained expansion), so reversing it restores the initial state of both system and surroundings exactly.
questions.trick: Reversible = retraceable exactly, passing only through equilibrium states throughout.

questions.q: For any spontaneous (naturally occurring, irreversible) process in an isolated system, the total entropy of the system
options: always increases (or, in the ideal reversible limit, stays the same)
questions.explanation: The second law implies the entropy of an isolated system can never decrease; it increases for irreversible (real, spontaneous) processes and stays constant only in the idealised reversible limit.
questions.trick: Second law: isolated-system entropy never decreases, rises for real irreversible processes.

questions.q: For a diatomic ideal gas with $\gamma=1.4$ and $R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, using $C_V=\dfrac{R}{\gamma-1}$, the molar specific heat at constant volume is
questions.trick: $C_V=R/(\gamma-1)$ — direct formula linking $\gamma$ and $C_V$.

questions.q: For a monatomic ideal gas with $\gamma=5/3$ and $R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$, using $C_P=\dfrac{\gamma R}{\gamma-1}$, the molar specific heat at constant pressure is
questions.explanation: $C_P=\dfrac{\gamma R}{\gamma-1}=\dfrac{(5/3)\times8.3}{2/3}=\dfrac{5}{2}\times8.3=20.75$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$.
questions.trick: $C_P=\gamma R/(\gamma-1)$ — companion formula to $C_V=R/(\gamma-1)$.

questions.q: The efficiency of a Carnot engine operating between two given temperatures depends only on
options: the working substance used (e.g. monatomic or diatomic gas)
the speed at which the cycle is carried out
the temperatures of the source and sink, and not on the nature of the working substance
questions.explanation: Carnot's theorem shows $\eta = 1-T_2/T_1$ is a universal result for any reversible engine working between two fixed temperatures, independent of the working substance.
questions.trick: Carnot efficiency depends only on the two temperatures, never on the gas used.

questions.q: A refrigerator has a coefficient of performance of 4 and extracts 800 J of heat from its interior in each cycle. The work that must be supplied to it per cycle is
questions.explanation: $\text{COP}=Q_2/W \Rightarrow W = Q_2/\text{COP} = 800/4 = 200$ J.
questions.trick: $\text{COP}=Q_2/W\Rightarrow W=Q_2/\text{COP}$ — rearrange and divide.

questions.q: For the same device operating between the same two temperatures, the coefficient of performance as a heat pump ($\text{COP}_{HP}=Q_1/W$) compared to its coefficient of performance as a refrigerator ($\text{COP}_{R}=Q_2/W$) is
questions.explanation: Since $Q_1=Q_2+W$, dividing by $W$ gives $\text{COP}_{HP}=Q_1/W=Q_2/W+1=\text{COP}_R+1$, so the heat-pump COP always exceeds the refrigerator COP by exactly 1.
questions.trick: $Q_1=Q_2+W\Rightarrow\text{COP}_{HP}=\text{COP}_R+1$ always, for same device/temperatures.

questions.q: A gas undergoes a cyclic process represented on a $P$-$V$ diagram by a rectangle, with pressure varying between $1\times10^5$ Pa and $3\times10^5$ Pa, and volume varying between $2\times10^{-3}$ m$^3$ and $5\times10^{-3}$ m$^3$ (cycle traversed clockwise). The net work done by the gas in one complete cycle is
questions.explanation: For a rectangular cycle, net work $=$ area enclosed $=\Delta P\times\Delta V=(3-1)\times10^5\times(5-2)\times10^{-3}=2\times10^5\times3\times10^{-3}=600$ J.
questions.trick: Rectangular cycle: net work $=\Delta P\times\Delta V$ (area of the rectangle).

questions.q: In the first law $\Delta Q=\Delta U+\Delta W$ (with $W$ = work done BY the gas), the work term $\Delta W$ during compression of the gas is taken as
options: negative, since the surroundings do work on the gas
questions.explanation: During compression the gas's volume decreases, so the gas does negative work on the surroundings (equivalently, the surroundings do positive work on the gas); by convention this is written as negative $\Delta W$.
questions.trick: Compression shrinks volume $\Rightarrow$ gas does negative work (surroundings push in).

questions.q: The Clausius statement of the second law of thermodynamics asserts that
options: heat cannot, by itself (without external work being done), flow from a colder body to a hotter body
entropy of the universe is constant
questions.explanation: The Clausius statement says spontaneous heat flow always occurs from hot to cold; making heat flow the other way (as in a refrigerator) requires external work to be supplied.
questions.trick: Clausius: heat never flows cold$\to$hot spontaneously, needs external work input.

questions.q: Two moles of an ideal diatomic gas are heated at constant pressure so that its temperature rises by 20 K ($R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$). The increase in internal energy of the gas is
questions.explanation: $C_V=\tfrac52R=20.75$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$ for a diatomic gas; $\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T=2\times20.75\times20=830$ J.
questions.trick: $\Delta U=nC_V\Delta T$ always, regardless of process — use diatomic $C_V=\frac52R$.

questions.q: For 2 mol of an ideal diatomic gas heated at constant pressure with a temperature rise of 20 K ($R=8.3$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$), the total heat absorbed by the gas (using $C_P=\tfrac72R$) is
questions.explanation: $C_P=\tfrac72R=29.05$ J mol$^{-1}$K$^{-1}$; $Q=nC_P\Delta T=2\times29.05\times20=1162$ J (consistent with $Q=\Delta U+W=830+332=1162$ J).
questions.trick: Isobaric: $Q=nC_P\Delta T$; cross-check via $Q=\Delta U+W$.

questions.q: A gas at pressure $2\times10^5$ Pa and volume $4\times10^{-3}$ m$^3$ is compressed isothermally to a volume of $2\times10^{-3}$ m$^3$. The new pressure is
questions.explanation: Isothermal: $P_1V_1=P_2V_2 \Rightarrow P_2 = \dfrac{2\times10^5\times4\times10^{-3}}{2\times10^{-3}} = 4\times10^5$ Pa.
questions.trick: Isothermal: $P_1V_1=P_2V_2$ — Boyle's law, cross-multiply directly.

questions.q: Which of the following thermodynamic quantities is a state function, i.e. depends only on the initial and final states of the system and not on the path taken between them?
options: none of these — all depend on the path
questions.explanation: Internal energy is a state function (it depends only on temperature for an ideal gas); heat and work, in contrast, both depend on the specific path (process) followed.
questions.trick: Only $U$ is path-independent (state function); $Q$ and $W$ both depend on path.

questions.q: A gas expands from the same initial state to the same final volume, once isothermally and once adiabatically. Compared to the isothermal case, the final pressure reached after the adiabatic expansion is
questions.explanation: Since the adiabatic curve is steeper than the isothermal curve through the same initial point ($PV^\gamma$ falls off faster than $PV=$ const), for the same volume increase the adiabatic final pressure is lower.
questions.trick: Same starting point, same $V$: adiabatic curve falls steeper $\Rightarrow$ lower final $P$.

questions.q: Unlike solids and liquids, an ideal gas does not have a single fixed specific heat capacity because
options: the specific heat of a gas depends on the process (e.g. constant volume vs constant pressure) it undergoes, since the work done varies with the path taken
questions.explanation: Because $Q=\Delta U+W$ and $W$ depends on the process followed, the heat needed to raise a gas's temperature by a given amount (and hence its specific heat) differs for, say, constant-volume and constant-pressure heating.
questions.trick: Gas specific heat isn't fixed because $W$ (hence $Q$) depends on the process.

questions.q: From $\eta_{Carnot}=1-\dfrac{T_2}{T_1}$, a Carnot engine can attain 100% efficiency only if
options: the sink temperature $T_2=0$ K (absolute zero), which is unattainable in practice
the working substance is a monatomic ideal gas
questions.explanation: $\eta=1$ requires $T_2=0$ K; since absolute zero can never actually be reached, no real (or even ideal Carnot) engine can achieve 100% efficiency, consistent with the Kelvin-Planck statement.
questions.trick: $\eta=1$ needs $T_2=0$ K, unreachable $\Rightarrow$ 100% efficiency is impossible.

questions.q: A Carnot engine operating between two temperatures has an efficiency of 40%. If the same engine is run in reverse as a refrigerator between the same two temperatures, its coefficient of performance is
questions.trick: Get $T_2/T_1$ from $\eta=1-T_2/T_1$, then $\text{COP}=T_2/(T_1-T_2)$.
